claims.text: Corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection in Q235 steel is governed by the formation and stability of a protective oxide layer.
Temperature influences the formation and stability of the protective oxide layer on Q235 steel.
Aggressive salt exposure influences the formation and stability of the protective oxide layer on Q235 steel.
Material composition influences the formation and stability of the protective oxide layer.
Q235 steel will be exposed to an aggressive salt environment at 700–900 °C.
The relevant structural mediator is a protective oxide layer.
Protection is controlled by the thermodynamic stability of corrosion products relative to fluorine potential.
The impurity level in the salt controls corrosion-product stability and corrosion behavior.
Aggressive salt exposure will reduce the corrosion rate of Q235 steel by 30% relative to air at 700 °C.
Aggressive salt exposure will reduce the corrosion rate of Q235 steel by 20% relative to air at 900 °C.
Q235 steel exposed in air at 700 °C and 900 °C is the reference condition.
The hypothesis is bounded to aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
The actual corrosion rate may depend on the particular composition of Q235 steel and of the salt environment.
The experiment will measure corrosion rate after aggressive salt exposure over 700–900 °C.
Failure to obtain at least a 20% reduction at 700 °C and a 15% reduction at 900 °C relative to air will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis claims applicability across room- and high-temperature regimes, but the intervention and boundary include only 700–900 °C and provide no room-temperature condition.

The predicted reductions are 30% at 700 °C and 20% at 900 °C, whereas the falsification thresholds are only 20% and 15%. Results below the stated predictions could therefore be treated as non-falsifying.
